title: Contractors, customers worried by cuts to Maryland energy efficiency rebates
summary: As state lawmakers move toward short-term reductions to the EmPOWER program, which helps homeowners pay for energy-saving improvements, residents and the businesses that rely on the program try to figure out what's next.
content:
by Christine Condon, Maryland Matters March 23, 2026

by Christine Condon, Maryland Matters March 23, 2026

Angie Norfolk still remembers the FaceTime call she received from her husband from their home’s crawlspace, showing destroyed wooden boards — right beneath their living room floor.

They had only just purchased their home on Maryland’s Eastern Shore. And now they faced thousands of dollars in repairs.

Norfolk and her husband had no idea that they would ultimately receive a $10,000 rebate from a Maryland energy efficiency program, allowing them to complete a host of extra improvements as they repaired their crawlspace, including new insulation, causing a noticeable dip in their most expensive energy bills, to the tune of a few hundred dollars.

“That was one of the good lights at the end of this tunnel,” said Norfolk, 39, whose home is in Grasonville. “Yeah, we had this bad situation, but we got all this new energy efficiency stuff.”

The Norfolks received their rebate in 2024 through EmPOWER Maryland, a fund that Maryland electric customers pay into via their electricity bills. But this year, legislators in Annapolis are discussing cuts to the EmPOWER program, which could shrink some of the rebates — and completely eliminate others, starting in 2027.

Lawmakers are making the changes to reduce the EmPOWER surcharge on customers’ bills. They argue that it’s one of the few ways to easily get a somewhat quick reduction on bills. Comparatively, trying to stabilize energy markets thrown out of whack by data center demands will take much longer, they say.

“We don’t have huge numbers of tools in the toolbox in terms of the short-term,” said Sen. Brian Feldman (D- Montgomery), chair of the Senate Education, Energy, and the Environment Committee, during a news conference Friday.

The broad energy bill that includes the EmPOWER changes, called the Utility RELIEF Act, passed the House of Delegates last week, and the Senate is expected to take it up this week. The overall package has the support of House and Senate leaders, as well as the governor. But it is still unclear whether the Senate will make any additional changes, including to the EmPOWER provisions of the legislation.

As legislators continue to hammer out just how drastically EmPOWER will be cut, environmentalists and consumer groups warn that short-term cuts to EmPOWER, even if they only last a few years as proposed, could ultimately result in increased utility bills for Maryland customers. With less energy-efficiency work — from home weatherization to appliance upgrades and smart thermostat installations — comes a greater demand for energy, and possibly more energy infrastructure.

Meanwhile, the contractors who use the program are bracing for the worst. For them, the rebates increase the number of customers willing to pull the trigger on costly repairs. If the rebates decrease, some of their employees could lose their jobs.

“I just left my accountant for two hours today trying to forecast what it would look like,” said Matthew Hargrove, owner of Total Home Performance, a contracting company based in Easton. “How much have we done in rebates last year? If we assume that we get less than half of that work, how does that relate to lost revenue and lost jobs?”

If lawmakers do make sizable cuts to EmPOWER, Hargrove said he expects a “mad dash” of customers hoping to take advantage of the rebates before they lapse. But he is concerned about hiring new staff members to address the surge in demand, because he might have to lay them off in January, after the EmPOWER cuts would take effect.

Even if the program is supposed to ramp back up after about three years, as the legislation proposes, Hargrove worries that contractors will have pared down their businesses by then, and turned away from some of the energy programs covered under EmPOWER.

“Apparently it can turn off at the flick of a switch, but it’s not going to be able to just be turned right back on,” he said.

YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE.

Feldman argues that the EmPOWER program has delivered less return on investment over time, because consumers have executed many cheaper changes, like installing LED light bulbs. Other home improvements covered under the program, such as installing heat pumps, are considerably more expensive.

“The light bulbs and all the things that were kind of in the front end of the program were very, very successful in terms of energy efficiency,” Feldman said. “Now, you’re talking about much bigger kinds of equipment and appliances and things that don’t — the [return on investment] is not quite as compelling.”

As of 2024 data, the programs remains cost-effective statewide, returning $2.21 in benefits for every one dollar spent, according to a report from the Maryland Public Service Commission, the state’s utility regulator.

But the EmPOWER surcharge has risen faster than inflation. In 2015, the average residential customer paid between $5 and $7 per month for EmPOWER. But in 2025, the average customer paid $15 to $20. And the fee can be higher for customers who use more energy in their homes.

To cut the program, lawmakers are actually planning to decrease the greenhouse gas reduction goals that accompany it. In addition, they are allowing utilities, which run EmPOWER programs, to count solar energy toward 20% of their goal, further reducing the energy efficiency rebates they would offer.

But they are also completely eliminating EmPOWER programs run by Maryland gas companies, leaving only the programs run by electric companies.

That change would wipe out the EmPOWER Maryland program administered by Washington Gas, which doled out about $7 million to customers for energy efficiency upgrades last year. In total, the program cost $14.3 million for 2025, because of administrative, marketing and evaluation costs.

“If there’s any opportunity to save some change on your monthly bill, we want to provide that information in front of our customers. EmPOWER is the most prevalent and the most popular conduit through which the company can do that. We would be very concerned if that went away,” said Joshua McClelland, manager of the company’s energy efficiency program.

Lawmakers have said that they are aiming to completely protect the EmPOWER programs that serve low-income customers. But because Washington Gas would no longer be able to charge customers to pay for its programming, it wouldn’t be able to offer energy efficiency perks to low-income consumers, either, McClelland said.

The Washington Gas program does reward customers for replacing old gas furnaces with new, more efficient appliances. Maryland legislators may be trying to discourage that practice because new gas appliances still represent a source of fossil fuel emissions, and instead encourage consumers to choose new electric heat pumps.

But the company argues that, if the rebate disappears, customers won’t necessarily electrify.

“They’re going to stay on gas, and they’re going to choose the more affordable, less efficient system,” McClelland said.

The gas side of the EmPOWER program run by Baltimore Gas & Electric doesn’t provide any rebates for new gas appliances, said BGE spokesperson Jane Ballentine. Instead, it mainly goes toward programs to reduce gas consumption, by improving insulation and air sealing, or reducing hot water usage.

The Washington Gas EmPOWER program also provides customers with free home energy efficiency kits, McClelland said, with things like new shower heads, weather stripping and caulk. And it allows customers with smart thermostats to join a “demand response” program, allowing their utility to adjust the temperature in their homes slightly, to reduce demand during peak periods.

Katie Mettle, a principal with Advanced Energy United, said she is particularly concerned about the loss of smart thermostat programs, which are “incredibly valuable” to the grid.

She points to a peak period last June, when PJM only had about 10 gigawatts of energy left to spare. But it used “demand response” programs to free up 4 gigawatts.

“In terms of how much energy that freed up, that’s kind of like adding 2.2 Calvert Cliffs nuclear plants to the PJM region,” Mettle said. Advanced Energy United represents a number of energy technology companies, which focus on solar, wind, battery storage, EVs and geothermal.

Energy companies also use their demand response programs to bid into energy markets, Mettle said, which further lowers costs for consumers by decreasing the energy supply needed.

“The cheapest electron is the one you don’t use, and that’s what makes demand response such an affordable way to help us meet our electricity needs,” Mettle said.

Sean Mallonee, who owns S.M. Mechanical, an HVAC contractor based in Baltimore County, said he retains 25 employees, and five of them are energy auditors.

He fears that, if EmPOWER is significantly cut, their workload will decline because fewer homeowners will request home energy audits, meaning he may have to reduce their pay.

“I’m going to have some really, really difficult conversations,” said Mallonee, president of the Heating & Air Conditioning Contractors of Maryland.

Mallonee said he wasn’t expecting a state like Maryland, seen as a leader for its climate goals, to walk back the EmPOWER program, which has significant greenhouse gas reduction benefits. To contractors, it feels like a mixed signal, he said.

“You have these companies that you almost invited … I take it personally,” Mallonee said.

Mallonee said he’s also frustrated for the customers who have paid into the EmPOWER program since its inception in 2008, and now may not be able to take advantage of rebates.

“Your piggybank’s gone. You’ve put all this money into the EmPOWER program, and you don’t get anything out of it,” Mallonee said.

Mary Dadds and her husband Alan, of Stevensville, called Total Home Performance because cold air was chilling a particular spot on their kitchen floor — and because their electric bills were soaring.

“I thought, ‘I’ve got to do something.’ Our electric bill was crazy high and I knew that it wasn’t going to do anything but go up farther because of everything that’s going on,” said Dadds, 73.

Dadds received a $10,000 rebate for her crawlspace insulation project, which made a big difference. The family might have pursued the work without the rebate, Dadds said, but they might have taken out a loan to do so, since they live on a fixed income.

“It was wonderful,” she said.
